newsitem.title: USA: Detroit combats annual "Devil's Night" arsons.
newsitem.headline: Detroit combats annual "Devil's Night" arsons.

text.p: City leaders on Monday once again have demolished abandoned houses, towed vehicles and mustered thousands of volunteers to dampen the annual Detroit ritual of "Devil's Night" arson fires one night before Halloween.

So far, 29,000 people have offered to wear special orange hats and watch neighbourhoods for suspicious activity, Michelle Zdrodowski, a spokeswoman for the city's 1996 anti-arson initiative, said on Monday.
"We really don't think we're going to have a problem reaching our 32,000 goal," she said.
Workers already met their target of leveling 850 abandoned houses. That is down from 1,000 last year, Zdrodowski said, because the city is also hauling away the debris for safety reasons.
As of Saturday, tow trucks had removed 2,712 abandoned vehicles, recovering 116 stolen vehicles in the process.
Holding down the number of fires during the three-day period of Oct. 29-31 has become a focus for Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer's administration.

Archer got burned in 1994, his first year in office, when he failed to match the emphasis his predecessor Coleman Young put on combating Halloween arson fires. That year, the number of fires jumped to 354 for the three-day period, the worst since the mid-1980s.
Last Halloween, Archer launched an "Anti-Arson Campaign," trying to de-emphasise the word "Devil's Night." The extra effort paid off, as the number of fires fell to 158 for the three-day period.

As it did in 1995, the Detroit City Council this fall passed an emergency ordinance that bans the sale of fuel in portable containers within city limits, except in emergencies, from Oct. 28 through midnight Oct. 31.
The city council also imposed a curfew from 6 p.m. Oct. 30 until 6 a.m. Oct. 31. Police arrested 210 youngsters for curfew violations during the same time a year ago.
